vignette:
Tane is a forty-two-year-old electrician who lives with his partner, Leilani, in a coastal town in Aotearoa. He was assaulted eight months ago, outside a petrol station on a Friday night. He had stopped to fill up after a late job wiring a new build, and three men jumped him from behind. He doesn't remember much of the beating-just the crack of his own ribs and the taste of blood. Someone stole his wallet and his phone, and left him unconscious on the concrete.

For the first few weeks afterward, Tane told himself he was fine. He took a week off work, then went back because the foreman needed him on a commercial site. But he couldn't stop scanning the carpark. Every time a car door slammed behind him, his shoulders would shoot up to his ears. His hands would shake on the wire strippers. Once, when a coworker touched his shoulder to ask for a tool, Tane swung around with his fist raised. He apologised, said he was just tired, but his heart kept pounding for an hour.

The nightmares started around the same time. He doesn't dream about the assault directly-mostly he sees faces floating toward him out of darkness, hears footsteps that don't stop. He wakes up drenched in sweat, convinced someone is in the room. Leilani has learned not to reach for him in the dark. She told him last week that she feels like she's sleeping next to a stranger. Tane knows she's right. He used to be easygoing, the kind of bloke who would laugh over a barbecue. Now he watches the door of every pub they pass. He stopped going to his uncle's fishing trip because the boat jetty had too many blind corners.

At work, his concentration has frayed. He double-checks circuits three times, then doubts himself. On a ladder last Tuesday, he heard a sudden bang from a nearby dumpster and nearly lost his balance. He held onto the beam so hard his fingers cramped. The foreman asked if he was okay, and Tane just nodded. He doesn't talk about it. He can't. The words get stuck in his throat like a physical blockage. When Leilani asks how his day was, he says, "Fine," and turns on the television to drown out the silence.

The most exhausting part is the hypervigilance. Tane checks the locks before he can fall asleep. He has started parking his van so that he can see the entrance of any building he enters. If a stranger walks too close behind him in a hardware aisle, he steps aside to let them pass-and then he feels shame, rage, a hot flush of something that makes him want to hit something. He hasn't hit anyone. But he has snapped at Leilani for leaving a window open, for making a sudden noise in the kitchen. Afterwards, he sits on the edge of the bathtub and stares at his hands.

He used to fix things. That was his pride: he could trace a faulty wire back to its source and make the lights come on again. Now he feels like a broken switch-live current, but no connection. The world used to feel solid. Now every shadow holds a threat, every unexpected sound is a prelude to pain. He carries the assault in his body: a tightness across his chest, a constant low-level tremor in his legs. He has started drinking two beers every night just to take the edge off, and sometimes three. Leilani hasn't said anything yet, but he sees her watching.

He doesn't know how to tell her that he feels like he is still lying on that concrete, waiting for someone to notice him.
